title: Who is speaking in Manu's book
hookLine: the Manusmriti opens with sages asking Manu, and Bhrigu speaking
carry: smriti is remembered, so ask who remembered it
tomorrow: does the law book ever bend its own rules? and for whom?
last: READ IT WHOLE. SAY WHAT IT SAYS.

lines: PICK ONE TEXT. READ IT CRITICALLY.
cards: The assignment lands on a Friday: senior seminar, pick one text and read it critically. Some kids pick a novel, some a well-known speech.
Priya stares at the list for a long time, then types in the book that guy in her comments keeps quoting: the Manusmriti. Her dad, Arjun, reads over her shoulder and says, dryly: bold.
Then he adds: you know who's actually talking in that book, right?

teach.h: SAGES ASK MANU FOR THE DHARMA.
teach.b: Here's the answer, and it's one to pass on. The Manusmriti opens like a scene.

Great sages come to Manu as he sits with a collected mind, honor him, and ask him to teach them the duties of every class of people. Manu agrees and starts at the very beginning, with the making of the world.
Then, still in the first chapter, he tells how the teaching reached him: the Creator taught it to him first, and he taught it to Marichi and the other first sages.
And now, he says, Bhrigu here has learned the whole of it from me, and he will tell it to you. Bhrigu, pleased, begins. So the book presents itself as a teaching handed down, teacher to student.
That frame carries a big Hindu idea in its very name.
The Veda is shruti, what was heard, held to be revealed to the ancient seers. A book like Manu's is smriti, what is remembered, handed down by people, one to the next.
That's why Hindu teachers have long weighed smriti against the Veda and against each other, and why a critical reader asks who did the remembering, for whom, and who wasn't in the room.
Now the week, in one breath. The Buddha, honored as Vishnu's form, his story still Buddhist. Descents beyond counting.
Kalki, still to come. The Kali age, with one door: sing the name. A wheel of ages turning back to truth.
And dharma with four sources, not one book.

how: Students of the dharma texts read the Manusmriti with its old commentaries and alongside other dharma books; readers today often begin by asking who the text speaks for and to.

o: the laws of Manu, framed as Bhrigu retelling them
a hymn the sages sang on the day Manu was born
a list of Vishnu's ten forms that Bhrigu kept

games.q: the week, one pair a day — tap the pairs.

s: after Kalki, the world simply ends
in the Bhagavata, the age of truth comes round again.
Kali the age and Kālī the goddess are different words
short vowels for the age, long ones for the goddess.
every Hindu list of the ten forms includes the Buddha
some lists count Balarama in his place.

games.q: a classmate says: Hindus count the Buddha as Vishnu, so Buddhists are basically Hindus. what's the fair reply?
o: some Hindu texts tell him that way; Buddhists tell him as their own teacher.
right: the Bhagavata settles it, so the two are one religion.
wrong: no Hindu text ever mentions the Buddha at all.
games.why: say whose telling it is: the Bhagavata and Jayadeva place him in Vishnu's line; Buddhists tell him as their teacher, and it's theirs to tell.

practice: Close your eyes and think of the first prayer, mantra or story about right and wrong you were ever taught. Who taught it to you? And who taught them?
That chain, teacher to student, is how smriti travels; Hindus call it parampara. If you weren't raised with prayers, pick any first lesson about what's right.
Just notice the faces in the chain, and notice too whose face is missing. Breathe with them for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: the laws of Manu, a smriti, what is remembered, which the book frames as Bhrigu passing on Manu's teaching to the sages.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Bhrigu, the sage who, in the book's own frame, retells Manu's teaching.

carryVoice: Carry this: smriti is remembered, so ask who remembered it, and who wasn't in the room. That's the week.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 1.1–4 (the great sages approach Manu and ask for the dharma)
Manusmriti 1.58–60 (Manu says Bhrigu learned the whole from him and will teach it; Bhrigu speaks)
Manusmriti 2.10 (shruti is the Veda; smriti the dharma texts)
